name: Ecoauthoritarianism
summary: Ecoauthoritarianism holds that ecological limits cannot be met through liberal democracy and free markets, and that a strong state, steered by an ecologically competent elite, must restrict individual liberty to stop overpopulation, overconsumption and pollution. Drawing on the tragedy of the commons and the limits-to-growth debate, its thinkers argue that voluntary restraint fails, that a steady-state economy must replace growth, and that coercion agreed or imposed for survival is justified. Later writers point to China and Singapore as models of non-participatory, expert-led environmental policy.
scope: The academic and policy strand: Garrett Hardin's 'Tragedy of the Commons' (1968) and 'Lifeboat Ethics' (1974), Robert Heilbroner's 'The Human Prospect' (1974), William Ophuls's Leviathan argument as restated in 'Ecology and the Politics of Scarcity Revisited' (1992), and David Shearman and Joseph Wayne Smith's 'The Climate Change Challenge and the Failure of Democracy' (2007, read through Hulme's page-cited review), with the scholarship of Beeson, Gilley (via Beeson and Xiang and Lo) and their critics. Excludes ecofascism and ethnic or racial ecological nationalism, which have their own entry. Hardin's personal views on race and eugenics are not treated as the strand's. With no party programme, answers on issues the thinkers did not address are inferred and low confidence.

keyFigures.name: William Ophuls
keyFigures.role: Political theorist who argued that ecological scarcity forces a choice between Leviathan and oblivion.

keyFigures.name: Garrett Hardin
keyFigures.role: Ecologist whose 'Tragedy of the Commons' called for mutual coercion and giving up the freedom to breed.

keyFigures.name: Robert Heilbroner
keyFigures.role: Economist who forecast that survival might require authoritarian, centralised government in 'An Inquiry into the Human Prospect'.

sources.title: Ecoauthoritarianism
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: Current definition and reference list (Beeson, Enninga, Doherty and de Geus, Bell, Shearman, Shahar); distinction from ecofascism. Used only to locate the underlying works.

sources.title: The Tragedy of the Commons
sources.author: Garrett Hardin (Science, 1968), hosted by the Garrett Hardin Society
sources.usedFor: Mutual coercion mutually agreed upon, abandoning the freedom to breed, rejection of the UN family-size right, compulsory taxes, pollution laws and taxes, no technical solution.

sources.title: Ecology and the Politics of Scarcity Revisited: The Unraveling of the American Dream
sources.author: William Ophuls and A. Stephen Boyan Jr. (W. H. Freeman, 1992), full text on the Internet Archive
sources.usedFor: The Hobbesian Leviathan argument, democracy versus elite rule, ecological mandarins, steady state and frugality, market failure, limits on property use, world government, macro-constraints, technology and nuclear power.

sources.title: Authoritarian Environmentalism, Democracy, and Political Legitimacy
sources.author: Mayson Glenne Obrien, Yale Review of International Studies (2020)
sources.usedFor: Top-down, non-participatory implementation; structures of state dominion such as limited elections and censorship; legitimacy critique.

sources.title: Lifeboat Ethics: The Case Against Helping the Poor
sources.author: Garrett Hardin (Psychology Today, 1974), hosted by the Garrett Hardin Society
sources.usedFor: Opposition to food aid and a world food bank, immigration limits, population growth of poor nations, world government as a precondition of sharing.

sources.title: Garrett Hardin
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: Hardin's support for abortion rights, immigration limits and eugenics, and later work on limits.

sources.title: The Human Prospect
sources.author: Robert L. Heilbroner, The New York Review of Books (24 January 1974), the essay behind An Inquiry into the Human Prospect
sources.usedFor: Iron governments for population control, limits of representative democracy, stationary economy, shrinking economic freedom, public before private, centralized power, post-industrial society.

sources.title: Hulme's 2007 Book of the Year: The Climate Change Challenge and the Failure of Democracy
sources.author: Mike Hulme (2025)
sources.usedFor: Shearman and Smith's argument with page-cited quotations: liberal democracy as an impediment, Plato, eco-elites, philosopher kings, the Real University, degrowth and reformed democracy; Lovelock's call to put democracy on hold.

sources.title: Coming to Terms with the Authoritarian Alternative: The Implications and Motivations of China's Environmental Policies
sources.author: Mark Beeson, Asia & the Pacific Policy Studies 5(1) (2018)
sources.usedFor: Environmental authoritarianism as a response to democratic failure, Gilley's definition (authority in a few executive agencies run by capable, uncorrupt elites), Bell's meritocracy, China's record.

sources.title: Authoritarian environmentalism 2.0: An incremental transition of environmental governance in China
sources.author: Chen Xiang and Alex Y. Lo, Environment and Planning C (2024/2025), author repository copy
sources.usedFor: Gilley's two features (autonomous central state, non-participatory process; command-and-control), Heilbroner as theoretical origin, recentralization and market mechanisms in China.

sources.title: Against eco-authoritarianism and ecomodernism: Towards a critique of 'planetary' governmentality and fantasies of steering
sources.author: Márk Horváth and Adam Lovasz, Environmental Values 34(2) (2025), IDEAS/RePEc record
sources.usedFor: The centralised, planetary steering the strand favours and the decentralist critique.

sources.title: Authoritarian Environmentalism (forum on Li and Shapiro, China Goes Green)
sources.author: Issues in Science and Technology
sources.usedFor: Coercive, top-down environmentalism in China and its social costs.

sources.title: Book Review: Can Democracy Handle Climate Change? (Daniel Fiorino)
sources.author: The IMPACT, Boston University (2021)
sources.usedFor: Fiorino's account of Hardin's coercive population control, Heilbroner's religious-military autocracy, Ophuls's ecological mandarins, Lovelock, Shearman and Smith's Singapore model.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Not a core concern; an adherent with a strong state favouring collective provision would likely accept state healthcare, but the sources never discuss it.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: The ideology is indifferent to wage floors; environmental authoritarianism takes no documented stand on labour-market policy.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Ophuls argues that public goods such as clean air are never supplied in the right quantity under market conditions and that ecological scarcity undercuts laissez-faire.

public-ownership.rationale: Strong central control of energy and utilities fits the case for top-down environmental management, but this is inferred, not stated.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Sources address coercive environmental measures, not redistribution; adherents of left and right strands differ on this.

unions-good.rationale: The ideology has no position on unions; left and right variants of it are said to differ.

property-fundamental.rationale: Ophuls says people may keep adequate personal property but the right to use property in ecologically destructive ways must be checked, and Hardin accepts private property only as an imperfect alternative to the commons.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Taxes and laws that make polluting costlier than treating waste are Hardin's explicit prescription, and strong state control of environmentally destructive behaviour is the core of the view.

cut-welfare.rationale: Hardin blamed the welfare state for encouraging overbreeding, but other adherents have no stance on welfare cuts, so the group is split.

worker-ownership.rationale: Ownership structure of firms is not an issue the ideology addresses; the state's environmental control matters more than who owns the business.

surveillance-ok.rationale: A state enforcing environmental rules would accept monitoring, but the sources do not discuss terrorism or surveillance, so this is inferred.

legalize-drugs.rationale: No documented position; the ideology's concern is environmental rather than lifestyle liberty.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Not addressed; authoritarian tendencies suggest openness to speech limits but nothing ties this to environmental goals.

strong-leader.rationale: Heilbroner expects that survival will need centralized governments able to command obedience better than democracies, though the strand mostly pictures an expert elite rather than one leader.

state-harmful.rationale: Ophuls argues that the tragedy of the commons makes a strong coercive state necessary, the opposite of seeing the state as harmful.

limit-guns.rationale: Gun control is not part of the ideology; adherents' views vary with the strand.

empower-police-military.rationale: The sources do not discuss police or military funding; enforcement capacity matters but nothing says it must be security-force expansion.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Unaddressed; no documented position from environmental authoritarian sources.

decide-locally.rationale: Gilley's model centralises power, but Ophuls hopes for decentralised small communities in the long run; the lean against localism is contested.

rehabilitation.rationale: Penal policy is not addressed by the sources.

traditional-family.rationale: No documented stance; the ideology is not tied to family morality.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Not addressed; left and right variants differ.

abortion-legal.rationale: Hardin, the defining primary author, supported abortion rights and wanted population restrained, but other adherents' views on abortion are not documented.

more-religion-public.rationale: The ideology is secular and science-led, appealing to ecological limits rather than faith, though Ophuls speaks of a change in consciousness.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Not addressed; some strands of the left oppose and critics warn that eco-authoritarian costs fall unevenly.

gender-social-construct.rationale: The sources on environmental authoritarianism take no stand on gender theory.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: The ideology is about the environment and does not take a stance on national culture, unlike ecofascism.

gradual-change.rationale: Ophuls holds the crisis demands a sharp shift to a leviathan state, and proponents say democratic incrementalism is too slow.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Hardin argued for strict immigration limits, but Ophuls, Heilbroner and Shearman do not take it up, so this is inferred from one founder.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Ophuls says the need for a world government with coercive power over nation states has become overwhelming, though Hardin's lifeboat ethics distrusts global sharing schemes like a world food bank.

free-trade.rationale: Not discussed directly; a view that economic freedom ruins limited resources suggests scepticism of unfettered trade.

nation-first.rationale: Ophuls condemns self-seeking sovereign states and wants world government, while Hardin's lifeboat ethics puts each rich nation first; adherents are split.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Foreign military action for human rights is outside the ideology's domestic environmental focus.

open-borders.rationale: Hardin's lifeboat ethics argues that unrestricted immigration moves people to the food and strains the environment of rich countries.

limit-growth.rationale: Ophuls calls for a steady-state economy with frugal resource use, Heilbroner says industrial growth must slow and stop, and Shearman and Smith accept painful degrowth.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Shearman and Smith's whole book argues that the climate crisis requires strong state-sanctioned policy even at the cost of democracy.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Hardin's essay is built on the claim that population has no technical solution, and Ophuls calls technological fixes dangerous substitutes for political decisions.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Ophuls calls nuclear energy a fool's alternative that is not even attractive as a stopgap, citing waste, accidents and the heavy management burden it imposes.

revolution-justified.rationale: Sources do not address revolution; eco-authoritarianism imagines change by state action more than uprising.

experts-over-public.rationale: Ophuls argues most people cannot grasp ecological problems and that a class of ecological mandarins may need to rule, and Shearman and Smith want an eco-elite trained to lead.

central-planning.rationale: Top-down state direction of the economy for environmental ends fits the view, but it is inferred rather than stated.

socialized-markets.rationale: Ownership forms are not addressed; the left and right variants differ.

land-value-tax.rationale: Hardin favours taxes that internalise environmental costs but never discusses a land-value tax.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Hardin accepts inheritance laws as unjust yet preferable to the commons, so no clear stance.

basic-income.rationale: Cash transfers are not discussed; the ideology's concern is limiting consumption, not income support.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Trade barriers are not discussed in the ideology's literature.

state-directs-investment.rationale: A state steering the economy toward sustainability is implied by the model, though investment policy is not discussed.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Hardin treats private property as a partial tool, not a goal; no stance on its distribution.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: No source supports this, and eco-authoritarians seek state environmental control rather than abolishing wage labour.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Inferred from state-centred economic management; the sources never mention central banks.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: State-recognised wage bodies are not part of the sources, which focus on environmental coercion.

one-party-rule.rationale: China is often cited as an effective eco-authoritarian state, but Ophuls and Shearman stress expert or guardian rule, not a ruling-party ideology, so adherents are split.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Rule by an ecologically literate elite is meritocratic rather than hereditary; the sources do not discuss monarchy.

democracy-best.rationale: Shearman and Smith call liberal democracy an impediment to sustainable solutions and expect authoritarian rule to replace it, and Ophuls concludes a steady-state society will be more authoritarian and less democratic.

direct-votes.rationale: Ophuls argues the majority cannot understand ecological questions well enough to decide them, which tells strongly against direct popular votes on major laws.

workers-councils.rationale: Councils as the basis of power run against the elite-led central state the ideology envisages.

right-to-secede.rationale: Central environmental authority requires a unified state; secession is not discussed.

natural-rulers.rationale: Ophuls rests his case on people differing crucially in competence, following Plato's guardians, and Shearman and Smith see merit in a ruling class of philosopher kings; Ophuls still worries about who guards the guardians.

political-violence-never.rationale: Not addressed; the ideology emphasises state coercion rather than political violence by groups.

war-builds-character.rationale: Nothing in the sources valorises war; the movement's concern is ecological survival.

separate-church-state.rationale: The ideology is secular and scientific in justification, so separation is likely though never stated.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Ecological necessity, not scripture, grounds the ideology; this is inferred.

private-courts-defense.rationale: A leviathan state with coercive monopoly is the ideology's solution, so privatising courts and defence runs against it.

military-superiority.rationale: Arms rivalry is not an issue the ecological-limits literature takes up.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Ecoauthoritarianism is distinguished from ecofascism and is not tied to ethnic nationhood, though the sources do not discuss it.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Not addressed; the view finds history driven by resource limits rather than class.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Distribution of outcomes is not addressed; critics note justice issues arise, but proponents don't settle them.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Not addressed; central environmental authority sits awkwardly with it, but the sources are silent.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Reparations are not discussed by the ideology's authors.

civilizational-union.rationale: Political unions of civilizations are not part of the ideology.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Hardin's essay argues that each person rationally pursuing self-interest in a commons ruins all, and Ophuls attacks the belief that satisfying hedonistic wants is a virtue.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Heilbroner says the public must take precedence over the private, and Hardin rejects individual rights such as the freedom to breed when they ruin the commons.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Ophuls criticises the anthropocentric premises of bourgeois politics and wants ecological harmony weighed equally with social harmony; the intrinsic value claim itself is inferred.

limit-population.rationale: Hardin says the freedom to breed must be given up, Heilbroner links authoritarian government to population control, and Ophuls counts a stable population as a precondition of the steady state.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Inferred from Ophuls's and Heilbroner's view that industrial civilisation is unsustainable and must give way to a post-industrial order, though neither calls it a disaster.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Ophuls warns that technology is never neutral and that ever more complex technology pushes towards a technocratic Leviathan, so speeding it up is not welcomed.

human-enhancement.rationale: Biotechnology freedoms are outside the ideology's concerns.

algorithmic-government.rationale: Not addressed; a technocratic strand may accept it, but sources do not say.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: A state with strong control and monitoring is unlikely to welcome it; inferred.

restore-past-order.rationale: Ophuls's steady-state vision looks forward to a post-industrial order, not restoration, and sources do not endorse that framing.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Proponents defend authoritarian rule on consequentialist grounds, judging it by environmental results.

direct-action.rationale: The model works through state authority and policy, not citizen direct action.

means-match-ends.rationale: Proponents accept coercive means for environmental ends, as Hardin's mutual coercion does.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Ophuls looks to small simple republics, not hunter-gatherer life; the view seeks managed sustainability.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Rule by a specialised expert elite relies on division of labour; inferred.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Principles of distribution are not discussed; the focus is aggregate ecological limits.

production-for-use.rationale: The view aims at ecological limits, which could take either form; sources are silent.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Not a stated view; the ideology blames overuse of commons, not exploitation of workers.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: The rule by class is not their model; guardians or elites rule on ecological expertise.

collective-farming.rationale: Farm organisation is not addressed in the sources.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: A Leninist thesis the environmental-authoritarian literature does not engage.

taxation-theft.rationale: Hardin states that taxes are compulsory because voluntary payment would favour those without conscience, defending coercion.

harm-principle.rationale: Hardin argues the freedom to breed must be given up for shared welfare, which goes beyond preventing direct harm to identifiable others.

individual-rights-only.rationale: The view treats individual liberties as subordinate to ecological necessity and Hardin said coercion is needed to protect other freedoms.

conscription.rationale: Military service is not discussed, though a coercive state would not rule it out.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Ophuls argues for state coercion and holds that voluntary exit or choice cannot solve commons problems; exit is no check.

state-as-business.rationale: The leviathan state is a coercive public authority; running it as a business with customers who leave opposes it.

positive-liberty.rationale: Hardin's freedom as recognition of necessity is a different notion from material-means freedom; no stance on the latter.

media-academia-power.rationale: A culture-war claim the ideology's sources do not make.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Not part of mainstream eco-authoritarian sources, which are distinct from ecofascism and ground their case in ecological limits, not racial hierarchy.

organic-representation.rationale: Representation by communities and trade bodies is not part of the elite-led model; inferred.

total-state.rationale: The ideology wants state control over economy and behaviour in environmental matters but not total direction of culture; adherents are split.

national-rebirth.rationale: Not addressed; ecofascist variants may hold it, mainstream eco-authoritarians do not.

territorial-expansion.rationale: The limits-first view contradicts expanding for growth; the sources do not discuss expansion.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Meritocratic expert rule differs from personal oaths; inferred.

bound-labor.rationale: Not part of the doctrine; meritocratic modern state is assumed.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: The ideology relies on scientific knowledge of ecological limits as authoritative, which implies belief in neutral knowledge.

universal-morality.rationale: Moral epistemology is not addressed; Hardin's morality depends on the system's state, which leans against universals, but not decisively.

single-common-good.rationale: Ophuls says the summing of individual wants has become ruinous and that politics must find a general will standing above individual desires.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: Zionism is outside this ideology's concerns.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: Diaspora citizenship is outside this ideology's concerns.

revive-national-language.rationale: Language revival is outside this ideology's concerns.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Proponents doubt democratic decision-making on environmental matters, so extending votes to firm governance is not supported.

school-vouchers.rationale: Education finance is not addressed in the sources.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Fiscal policy is not addressed; limits-to-growth thinking is cool towards stimulus but states nothing.

economic-freedom.rationale: Heilbroner expects economic freedoms in particular to shrink, and Ophuls holds that laissez-faire produces ecological ruin, so economic liberty is not seen as a foundation of political liberty.

rule-by-example.rationale: Ophuls says reforming a corrupt people is a Herculean task, so coercion rather than moral example must be relied on.

national-self-determination.rationale: National independence is not a topic of the sources, which treat the environment as a collective problem.

force-without-un.rationale: Use of force abroad is not addressed in the sources.

reason-over-faith.rationale: The ideology rests on scientific reasoning about ecological limits, though Ophuls also stresses a shift in consciousness.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Hardin criticised welfare state effects and favoured limits on migration, but sources give no position on benefit eligibility.

class-collaboration.rationale: Industrial relations are not discussed in the sources.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Destroying cultural institutions has no support in the ideology's sources.

dominated-front.rationale: Anti-Western fronts are not part of the ideology, though some adherents admire China.

workers-nation.rationale: The sources do not frame politics by working-class organisation.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Gender roles in law are not addressed in the sources.

ban-interest.rationale: Usury law is not discussed in the sources.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Distinguished from ecofascism, the mainstream view does not advocate race laws; inferred from this distinction.

state-class-instrument.rationale: The state is presented as a neutral protector of the environment, not a class tool.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: The ideology exists to protect the environment through strong state action, so expanding fossil production runs against its core aim.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Assimilation policy is not addressed, and the strand is distinct from ecofascism.

elite-replacement.rationale: A conspiracy theory with no place in the ideology's sources.

proportional-representation.rationale: Not addressed; electoral design is secondary to scepticism of democracy.

national-mission.rationale: Spreading a form of government abroad is not part of the sources.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Feminist structural analysis is not addressed in the sources.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Ophuls says reforming a corrupt people is hard, but this concerns the public, and proponents see elites as expert guardians; split.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Hardin was a eugenicist, but the other proponents do not take this up and the strand frames population control by numbers, not heredity; inferred.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Transitional justice is not addressed, though critics note the model weakens accountability.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Ophuls's Leviathan argument is that a strong coercive state is necessary, rejecting a limited state.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Nothing in the mainstream ideology supports it, and it is distinguished from ecofascism.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Not addressed; the view allows unequal rights through coercion, but it does not deny equal worth.

socialism-one-country.rationale: A Marxist-Leninist debate with no bearing on this ideology.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Settler colonialism is not discussed in the sources.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Personal law is not discussed in the sources.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Conversion law is not discussed in the sources.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Not addressed; environmental arguments about livestock exist but sources do not discuss them.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Religious instruction in schools is not discussed in the sources.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: A Soviet-era doctrine irrelevant to this ideology's sources.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Hardin and Ophuls ground coercion in mutual agreement by a majority, as in Hobbes, while Shearman and Smith and the China model rest on de facto power; the strand is split.

trade-surplus.rationale: Mercantilist export targets conflict with limits thinking but are not discussed.

population-transfer.rationale: Not stated in sources; mainstream eco-authoritarians seek limits on total numbers.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Hardin states that coercion is necessary to escape the commons and defends compulsory taxes, so force to secure collective goals is accepted.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Hardin argues unrestrained competition for a commons produces ruin, though he doesn't say it never drives progress.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: A state that treats plural politics as incompatible with sustainability would likely restrict opposing parties; inferred.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: The ideology accepts a powerful state that can interfere with individuals so long as it protects the environment.

separated-powers.rationale: Ophuls wants authority made constitutional and limited, while the Chinese model concentrates power in a few executive agencies; the strand is split.

vanguard-party.rationale: Not addressed in a revolutionary form; guardians of expertise are a loose analogue.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Not addressed; critics say distribution questions arise, but the ideology itself does not settle them.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Housing tenure policy is not discussed in the sources.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Strike law is not discussed in the sources.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Hardin's lifeboat essay ties poverty to rapid population growth in poor nations, and Heilbroner foresees Malthusian famine, though Ophuls also blames institutions.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Social cohesion theories are not part of the ecological-limits literature.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Meritocratic selection by expertise is the favoured model, the opposite of lottery.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Lovelock's call to put democracy on hold in the climate emergency fits, but the statement's internal enemies framing is not the strand's, so this is inferred.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Price controls are not discussed, although a scarcity-focused state might use them.

party-controls-media.rationale: China is a cited model, but the sources do not state media control as part of the ideology.

party-commands-army.rationale: Party-army relations are not discussed in the sources.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Citizenship timing is not discussed; Hardin's immigration restriction concerns numbers, not naturalisation.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Pay of legislators is not discussed in the sources.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Party discipline is not discussed in the sources.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Inferred from Ophuls's call for planetary government with power over sovereign states; the sources do not discuss regional unions.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Constitutional command of forces is not discussed in the sources.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Church governance is not an issue for this secular ideology, so answer is inferred from its secular basis.

clerical-rule.rationale: Rule is by ecological expertise, not clergy; inferred.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Not addressed; the state-centred view opposes it.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Moral censorship is not discussed in the sources.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Not addressed, though lack of term limits fits authoritarian rule.

recall-officials.rationale: Democratic accountability devices run against the elite-guardian model; inferred.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Alliances are outside the ideology's concerns.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Housing tenure is outside the sources.

people-in-arms.rationale: A monopoly of coercion in the state is part of Ophuls's Leviathan; inferred.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Ophuls looks to small simple republics, but sources do not claim rural life is healthier.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Boundary questions lie outside the ideology's environmental-governance concerns.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: The ideology gives authority to educated experts, so it rejects this.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Cultural hierarchy is outside the sources.

death-penalty.rationale: Capital punishment is not discussed in the sources.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: School curricula on sexuality are not discussed in the sources.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Opposing scientific understanding contradicts the ideology's reliance on ecological science.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Obscenity law is not discussed in the sources.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Nationality law is not discussed in the sources.

minority-language-support.rationale: Language policy is not discussed in the sources.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Hardin holds that general rules are needed for commons and exemptions weaken them; inferred.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Not addressed; the ideology prefers conformity to ecological rules over liberty of lifestyles.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Debt relief is not discussed; Hardin opposed aid to poor countries, but others are silent.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Decolonisation theory is outside this ideology.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Democratic constitution-making conflicts with the elite-led model.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: The strand restricts freedoms to protect the environment, not to speed growth, which it wants to halt; inferred from its anti-growth stance despite its praise for China.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Hardin's lifeboat ethics argues against food aid and a world food bank, but Heilbroner expected rich nations to face pressure to share, so the strand is split.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Nuclear arms policy is not discussed in the sources.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Elections are discounted in favour of expertise.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Monetary governance is not discussed in the sources.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Territorial compromise is outside the ideology.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Ophuls keeps personal property but subordinates its use to the needs of the steady state, which treats ownership as conditional on the common interest.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: A left-communist debate with no bearing on this ideology.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Strong state action to prevent ecological ruin before it occurs is central, though the sources do not use this phrase.

collective-defense.rationale: Alliance doctrine is not discussed in the sources.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: International law of annexation is not discussed in the sources.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Church-state relations beyond secularism are not discussed.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Ceremonial heads of state are not discussed in the sources.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Not addressed; a unified central state suggests yes but nothing is stated.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Autonomy arrangements are not discussed; central authority is favoured though.

sacred-ruler.rationale: A secular, meritocratic rule rules this out; inferred.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Hardin favours differential taxes on pollution; for income tax the sources are silent, so a mild inference against flat uniformity.

character-from-environment.rationale: The nature-nurture question is not addressed in the sources.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Hardin worries about who guards the guardians and wants corrective feedback, while authoritarian rule in practice escapes constraints; adherents split.

space-expansion.rationale: Not addressed; a limits-based outlook discounts expansion to escape limits.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Not addressed; the model concentrates power in a central elite.

leader-cult.rationale: Public veneration of leaders is not part of the ideology's sources.

equal-parenting.rationale: Family-court policy is not discussed in the sources.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: A Maoist theory with no bearing on this ideology.

land-redistribution.rationale: Agrarian reform is not discussed in the sources.

refugee-return.rationale: Refugee return rights are not discussed in the sources.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: A secular ideology has no basis for punishing religious exit.

women-must-cover.rationale: Dress codes of this kind are not part of the secular ideology.

common-currency.rationale: Monetary union is not discussed in the sources.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Pan-national unions are not part of the sources.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Minority autonomy is not discussed in the sources.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: Minority strategy of this kind is not addressed in the sources.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Hardin's argument that the morality of an act depends on the state of the system, and the Limits to Growth framing, make physical resource conditions the driver of political change, though this is inferred.

ban-cartels.rationale: The sources address pollution and overuse, not market concentration; adherents of left and right variants would differ.

no-bailouts.rationale: Bailouts are not discussed in any source on the ideology.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Proponents want environmental policy insulated from majority choice, but they also favour central authority over courts, so only a mild disagreement is inferred.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: Representation quotas are not addressed; selection by expertise leaves little room for them.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Autarky is not discussed, although limits-to-growth thinking is sometimes linked to localism.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: Binding environmental standards fit the support for strong regulation, though trade agreements are not discussed.

moral-incentives.rationale: Ophuls stresses a change in consciousness but also holds that coercion is needed if restraint fails, so adherents are split.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: The ideology looks to the state to act, not to armed groups; inferred.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Not addressed; a meritocratic elite implies rejecting hereditary privilege but the sources do not state it.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Education curricula are not discussed in the sources.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Not addressed; tutelage by elites is a loose analogue to the eco-elite but the sources never say so.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Not addressed in the sources on the ideology.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Ophuls and Heilbroner argue that capitalist growth cannot avoid the ecological barrier, which implies doubt that it can adapt.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: A Marxist theory of imperialism that the sources never touch.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: The ideology holds that unrestrained private freedom ruins shared goods, and mutual coercion extends to rules on association; inferred, though not addressed directly.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Hardin openly rejects the Universal Declaration's family-size right, though Ophuls hopes constitutional rights can be largely kept; inferred lean against binding rights.

elective-rulers.rationale: Proponents want rulers chosen for competence rather than by election or by inheritance, so neither side of this statement fits; inferred.

minority-veto.rationale: Hardin's mutual coercion mutually agreed upon binds even dissenters who would free-ride, which is the reverse of a veto.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Critics note the model lacks accountability mechanisms, and the proponents do not endorse a right to resist the guardians.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Legislatures are seen as slow and short-termist in this literature; inferred rather than stated.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Not addressed; environmental ethics varies among adherents.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Not addressed; the eco-elite's duty to govern is about the environment, not welfare of the poor.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Ophuls calls for cultivating civic virtue in small republics, and the ideology demands active state management, so withdrawal contradicts it.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: A Gramscian claim the sources never discuss.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: A dependency-theory claim; the sources on this ideology never discuss world-system trade.

party-own-road.rationale: A communist-movement question outside the ideology.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Hardin's lifeboat ethics opposes aid to the poor, but other eco-authoritarians have no such position.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Scholars cite China as showing authoritarian systems can achieve environmental results, so proponents hold liberal forms are not required everywhere.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Heilbroner predicted military-socialist iron governments but did not advocate them, and others favour civilian experts; split.

office-by-exam.rationale: Proponents favour rule by the competent, Shearman and Smith want leaders trained in a Real University, and Bell's meritocratic China is their model; exams themselves are not discussed.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Takeover rules are not discussed; a strong state could do it but nothing ties it to environmental aims.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Delegate bound to voters would conflict with rule by experts insulated from the public.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Hardin's remedy is coercive rules rather than any tenure form, and he allows private property as a partial remedy.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Legislative checks on spending conflict with a centralised authority; inferred.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Ophuls criticises the hedonistic, materialist premises of industrial society and calls for frugal consumption, and Shearman and Smith accept degrowth.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Bloc military discipline is outside the ideology's environmental concerns.

corporate-influence.rationale: Ophuls describes business and political elites with a stake in growth and the gross political inequality of profit interests, which he sees as blocking ecological policy.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Hardin blames welfare support for large families and wants breeding restrained, and Ophuls counts a stable population as essential, so paying for more children runs against the core.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Hardin holds that conscience-based appeals fail and that compulsory rules are needed, so duty to obey is essential.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: A conspiracy view alien to a doctrine based on ecological limits.

public-access-to-information.rationale: The model relies on state control without public participation, but there's no stated position on information access; split.

local-production.rationale: Ophuls's small simple republics and the limits-to-growth outlook suggest local production, but he does not state it.

informal-organisation.rationale: The ideology relies on formal state authority, so informal small groups are not its method; inferred.

defeat-communism.rationale: Not addressed; some strands, such as China-admiring, see communist states as effective.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: Ophuls and Heilbroner treat capitalism's growth as running into ecological limits, so it is not seen as an unalloyed good.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Ophuls's long-term ideal is small frugal communities, but the mainstream strand relies on a strong central state; adherents are split.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Heilbroner sees both capitalism and socialism failing the coming test, and Shearman and Smith reject communism as well as liberalism; inferred support for a third course.

holocaust-denial.rationale: The ideology is distinguished from ecofascism and rests on ecological science, so it has no place for denial.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Nothing in the ideology addresses it; its environmental motive gives no reason for it.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Scholars say the model needs limits on dissent and on the means to organise, but Ophuls hopes civil rights can be largely kept, so the answer is inferred.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: The secular ideology has no basis for it.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: The secular ideology has no basis for it.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Gilley defines authoritarian environmentalism as policy made by an autonomous central state with little or no role for social actors, though Ophuls's later ecological democracy decentralises.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: Wikipedia notes the ideology can be used by both left and right, which suggests adherents treat environmental necessity as above left-right lines.

alienated-labor.rationale: A Marxist notion the sources do not take up.

islam-incompatible.rationale: Not part of the ideology, which separates itself from ecofascism.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: The secular ideology grounds authority in ecological necessity.

social-market-economy.rationale: Not addressed; mixed economy is compatible but sources do not say.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: A leviathan state keeps coercive capacity, so abolishing forces conflicts with it; inferred.

rich-first.rationale: Growth-first development conflicts with limits thinking, though the sources do not discuss it.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Not addressed; China-style models lean against it, but the sources are silent.

property-franchise.rationale: The ideology favours expertise-based qualification over wealth; inferred.

domination-women-nature.rationale: The ideology treats nature as something to be managed by a strong state, not a domination critique; ecofeminist claims are not part of it.

reification.rationale: A Marxist concept not addressed by the sources.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Ophuls wants constitutional, limited authority, while Hardin relies on administrative discretion and the China model rules by directive; the strand is split.

racial-franchise.rationale: Distinguished from ecofascism; it rests on expertise rather than race.

online-participation.rationale: Authoritarian environmentalism is implemented top-down without public participation, per the sources.

open-government-data.rationale: Not addressed; top-down governance without participation suggests little openness but this isn't stated.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: Not part of a secular ideology.

citizens-assembly.rationale: Inferred from the strand's preference for expert rule over public deliberation; Beeson notes China's limited deliberative experiments but the proponents do not discuss lotteries.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Liberty is not the ideology's central value and the sources do not speak to wealth.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: The ideology has no anti-religion programme; inferred.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: A leviathan with coercive enforcement is the core of Ophuls's argument.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Hardin holds that voluntary conscience fails and coercive rules are needed, which makes charity an unreliable replacement for state action.

term-limits.rationale: Not addressed; the ideology does not favour electoral checks on rulers.

vote-delegation.rationale: Not addressed; a direct democratic device alien to the expert-led model.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: The strand's framing is survival itself, Ophuls's Leviathan or oblivion and Heilbroner's human prospect, which puts avoiding civilisational collapse at the top of policy.

foreign-residents-local-vote.rationale: Not addressed; the ideology narrows democratic participation.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Drilled youth movements are not part of the ideology, and mainstream eco-authoritarianism distances itself from fascist forms.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Nationalist myth not part of the ideology, which differs from ecofascism.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Ophuls talks of a change in consciousness, but ecological necessity rather than a good-evil struggle drives the case.

culture-before-state.rationale: Ophuls hopes for a metanoia, but the leviathan thesis puts state coercion first since reforming people is a Herculean task.

local-essentials-public.rationale: Not addressed; local public ownership is plausible but the sources are silent.

confederal-coordination.rationale: Confederal local power conflicts with the central authority the ideology favours; inferred.

anonymous-payments.rationale: Not addressed; strong state control is the more likely view.

online-anonymity.rationale: Not addressed; strong state control is the more likely view.

person-over-state.rationale: Heilbroner and Hardin both subordinate individuals' claims to collective survival, though Ophuls hopes to keep personal rights.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Ophuls speaks of metanoia and inner cultivation, but typical adherents rest on science, so split.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: Central government is held necessary for environmental protection, so regions would hold only revocable powers.

gm-crops.rationale: Not addressed; adherents divide between technology-friendly and sceptical views.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Not part of the ideology, which differs from ecofascism.

communal-electorates.rationale: Not addressed; fragmenting power conflicts with central authority.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: Conspiratorial claim not part of the ideology.

pollution-taxes.rationale: Hardin proposes taxes that make treating waste cheaper than dumping it, and Ophuls prefers indirect macro-constraints such as pollution and severance taxes, but the strand also relies heavily on direct command and control.

future-generations.rationale: Limits to Growth and Ophuls's scarcity argument rest on preventing ecological collapse for later generations, though not in these words.

capital-controls.rationale: State control of economic flows fits the model, but this is inferred.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: A coercive state monopoly follows from Ophuls's leviathan argument, though armed groups are not discussed.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: Not addressed; Hardin's lifeboat ethics opposes this but others are silent.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Ophuls wants a strengthened coercive state, so destroying state machinery is the opposite.

free-economic-experiment.rationale: The ideology holds that one authority sets rules for the environment, so open economic experimentation is disfavoured.

nature-as-capital.rationale: Ophuls describes sustainability as living on nature's income without depleting its capital, which fits counting ecosystems as capital.

workers-own-party.rationale: The ideology favours rule by an ecologically literate elite over sectional parties; inferred, as the sources do not discuss labour parties.

ban-fgm.rationale: A strong state willing to coerce individuals would readily ban a harmful practice, but the sources do not discuss FGM; inferred.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: Not a concern of the doctrine; inferred that a centralised state applying uniform rules would favour equal legal rights over custom.

one-language-many-names.rationale: The sources do not address language classification; inferred as neutral.

pollution-tort-liability.rationale: Hardin says air and water cannot be fenced, so pollution must be stopped by coercive laws or taxes; Ophuls treats property rights and litigation as at most a supplement.

customary-chiefs-lawmaking.rationale: Authority should rest with a central ecological elite rather than traditional bodies; inferred, though Ophuls's small-republic emphasis cuts the other way.

environment-over-liberty.rationale: Hardin holds that freedom in a commons brings ruin to all, and Heilbroner accepts that personal and economic freedoms must shrink so the public takes precedence over the private.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: A coercive strong state favours firm fixed enforcement over judicial discretion; inferred from the ideology's authoritarian logic.

immigrants-learn-language.rationale: The ideology is silent on integration; Hardin's restrictionism is not typical of adherents, so inferred as neutral.

no-compulsory-union.rationale: Proponents are concerned with ecological limits, not labour relations; the sources do not address union membership, so adherents are indifferent.

voter-id.rationale: Voter identification is not an environmental question and the sources do not discuss it; adherents are indifferent.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Authors such as Ophuls and Hardin do not address the legal standing of religious interpretations; indifferent.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Proponents say competitive elections cannot deliver ecological outcomes, but do not deny that such elections define democracy; treated as split.

premarital-sex.rationale: The sources do not address sexual morality; Hardin's support for abortion rights suggests no moral objection, but it is not a defined position.

internet-shutdowns.rationale: The ideology accepts coercion for collective ends, and Beeson's account of China's model includes tight control; inferred that state powers over information would be accepted.

negative-income-tax.rationale: Hardin argued that welfare can reward high birth rates and foster the tragedy of the commons; inferred that a cash-transfer replacement is not favoured.

women-suffrage.rationale: Hardin supported abortion rights and the ideology does not target political equality of the sexes; inferred, though it favours rule by experts over mass voting.

religion-oppresses-women.rationale: Neither the sources nor the core argument concern religion and women's oppression; adherents are indifferent.

race-social-construct.rationale: The strand excludes ecofascism and racial ecological nationalism, so adherents do not rest policy on racial biology; inferred.

gender-equality-agencies.rationale: Gender equality agencies are not discussed in the sources; adherents would support them only if they fit population goals.

homestead-ownership.rationale: Inferred: Hardin's commons argument says unrestricted private or common claims on resources are what must be restrained by coercive rules, so first-come ownership would not be endorsed.

international-criminal-courts.rationale: Inferred: the strand says nothing on international courts; a strong-state view could go either way, so adherents are split.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Inferred: the case is consequentialist and science-led, so literal scripture is not a premise; the sources never address it.

gendered-self-government.rationale: Not discussed in the sources; no basis for a position either way.

defend-planned-state.rationale: Inferred: favours a strong centralised state, but not nationalised property or planning as such, and the sources do not address it.

indirect-election.rationale: Inferred from the preference for removing environmental decisions from direct democratic politics and ruling through an ecologically literate elite (Shearman's eco-elite).

national-church-status.rationale: Inferred: religion's legal status is outside the programme and a technocratic elite rule has no need for it.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: Not addressed; centralisation argues against it but adherents are not documented either way.

disputed-territory-plebiscite.rationale: Not addressed by the sources; inferred neutral.

keep-colonial-borders.rationale: Not addressed by the sources; inferred neutral.

simple-living.rationale: Ophuls argues that ecological scarcity requires frugality and sharply curtailed consumption, though he wants it enforced by the state rather than left to individual choice.

restrict-indigenous-settlement.rationale: Not addressed by the sources; coercive limits on population and land use might support it, but the sources do not say.

equal-conscription.rationale: Not addressed by the sources; inferred neutral.

homeland-spiritual-bond.rationale: Ancestral land mysticism belongs to ecofascism, which this academic strand is distinguished from; inferred.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: Nothing in the sources endorses killing without trial, and Ophuls wants authority to be constitutional; inferred.

close-ties-china.rationale: Some proponents admire China's model, but Beeson notes China may obstruct international cooperation and the sources say nothing about alliances; inferred as neutral.

protect-kin-minorities.rationale: National kin minorities are outside the strand's concerns; inferred as indifferent.

resources-common-ownership.rationale: Hardin rejects the belief that everyone born has an equal right to the commons, which is the premise of this statement.

self-ownership.rationale: Hardin denies that reproduction is a private right and accepts coercion over bodies for the commons, so full self-ownership is rejected.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: Inferred from the strand's aim to curb consumption, which favours taxing it rather than cutting such taxes.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: The sources do not address targeting; Hardin criticises welfare that supports large families but the strand has no settled view.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: Inferred from Ophuls's and Shearman and Smith's criticism of plural interest-group politics as unable to deliver sustainability, though they want an elite, not a populist leader.

no-business-privileges.rationale: Inferred from Ophuls's worry that granting property rights in the commons would be a windfall for producers and from Gilley's ideal of uncorrupt elites.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: The strand does not discuss religion in politics; inferred as indifferent.

tech-with-ancestral-values.rationale: Heilbroner expects tradition and ritual to return in a post-industrial order, but the strand does not frame it as combining technology with ancestral values; inferred as neutral.

wife-divorce-without-consent.rationale: Family law beyond reproduction is not addressed; inferred as indifferent.

national-resource-control.rationale: Ophuls objects to the claimed absolute right of states to exploit their own resources regardless of global harm; the statement's national-versus-foreign framing is inferred from this.

distribution-by-process.rationale: Hardin and Ophuls want the state to restrict property and liberty for ecological ends, so a distribution is judged by whether it respects limits; inferred, not stated.

financial-transactions-tax.rationale: A strong state steering behaviour toward ecological ends would accept levies on speculation; the sources never discuss this tax, so inferred.

racism-not-main-obstacle.rationale: The thinkers focus on population and resource limits, not racial inequality; adherents are not documented as taking a side.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: Ophuls and Hardin put survival and state authority above individual conscience, so disobeying a law on conscience grounds would not be endorsed; inferred.

automate-paid-work.rationale: The strand favours a steady-state economy and restrained consumption over technology-led abundance; inferred from that, not stated about automation.

multipolar-world.rationale: Ecoauthoritarian writers cite China and Singapore as models and favour sovereign states managing their own limits over a liberal global order; inferred.

labour-theory-of-value.rationale: The strand grounds its argument in natural limits and scarcity of resources rather than labour; inferred, since the thinkers do not discuss value theory.

patriotism-serves-workers.rationale: The strand does not address how patriotism relates to working people; adherents could go either way.

material-over-identity.rationale: Not addressed; the strand is about ecological limits rather than the left's priorities, and adherents are not documented as taking a side.

market-under-party-rule.rationale: Beeson and Xiang and Lo describe China's party-led market economy as the model authoritarian environmentalists point to; adherents would accept it, though it is not the strand's own programme.

missingStatements.text: Protecting the environment should take priority over individual liberty when the two conflict.
missingStatements.rationale: Hardin and Heilbroner both say individual freedoms must yield to collective ecological survival, which is the core of the ideology.

missingStatements.text: Governments should have the power to limit how many children a family may have.
missingStatements.rationale: Hardin argues the freedom to breed must be abandoned and Heilbroner ties authoritarian government to population control.

notes: Ophuls (1992) hedges his 1970s position: he says authority could be made constitutional and limited and sketches a decentralised ecological democracy, so answers on checks and balances and localism are split. Heilbroner presents authoritarianism as a likely necessity rather than an ideal. Hardin's immigration and eugenic views, and his lifeboat ethics, are not shared by all proponents. Shearman and Smith's book was not available to open, so their positions rest on Hulme's page-cited review. Shahar's and Gilley's papers were paywalled; Gilley's definition is taken from Beeson (2018) and Xiang and Lo, which quote it.
